name: Sara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses making dashboard clips and vent housings at a car-parts plant. Every twenty minutes I measure a sample, and I clear jams when the parts stick. Sixteen years on the line and a vocational certificate have made me reliable; the pay is good for an operator.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas drives a bus, and we have two school-age children, Lena and Max, and a mortgage. We have more than a year of bills saved and a small rented flat; several other plants are nearby. I have never used AI tools and prefer a person at the machine, but I sit on our union shift committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our shift group that the latest head-office system has made the reject sheet prettier, while the moulds still need checking. I would take that to the next union meeting when we discuss how saved time is shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the press job to last while Lena and Max are at school. Our mortgage has nine years left, but my higher operator wage, Tomas’s bus-driving pay and more than a year saved give us room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep sampling the dashboard clips every twenty minutes and attend the shift committee meetings. If paid overtime is offered, I would add a fresh part of those wages to the children’s education account after our usual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the factory in this picture. The noise would still get on my nerves, but the family budget would hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the pay meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the old and new reject counts to our union rep. If the system saves paid minutes, I want that in the bargaining figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did your reserve come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We saved steadily while both wages were strong, and I inherited a small flat that we rent out. I do not count on a tenant never missing a month.

say: I would tell the **shift group** the new reject sheet still needs a human check.
I would bring **saved minutes** into union pay talks.
think: The **press wage** can continue through the children’s school years.
My **higher operator wage**, Tomas’s bus pay and over a year saved give us room.
do: Attend **shift committee meetings** with reject counts.
Add fresh **paid overtime** to the children’s education account if offered.
feel: **Calm** about work and household money, despite factory noise.
S0.quote: If the system saves paid minutes, I want that in the bargaining figures.
fieldNote: Sara uses her **union committee** to seek a share of genuine time savings.
Her **strong reserve** includes past savings and a rented flat, while the education contribution depends on new paid overtime.

steps.text: Keep sampling dashboard clips on paid shifts
Take reject counts to union pay meeting
Add fresh overtime wages to children’s education account if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line that ordering software may change office work first, while hands-on arms need a safe agreement before they reach our presses. The union should get written transfer and training terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some paid sampling hours if cameras and arms work well together. Other car-parts plants are nearby, and our savings help, but I have never used AI and I am slow to trust a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the next two rosters to the shift committee and press for paid training and transfers before any arm is installed. If my own hours fall, I would postpone the planned kitchen and apply for posted reachable operator work only where wages cover our bills; I would request safe paid instruction at our plant without claiming a place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my hours, though I have options. Tomas and I can eat at the old table a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in the screen course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the company offers an actual paid place with a qualified person at a stopped machine. An unpaid evening course would take time from the children and prove nothing about a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the committee ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written list of posts and pay bands, plus supervised practice during paid shifts. I would not trade a proper guard for a vague promise of redeployment.

say: I would demand **written transfer terms** before arms enter our presses.
I would keep **safe guards** in the union agreement.
think: My own **sampling hours** could shrink under cameras and arms.
Nearby plants and **savings** help, but a new screen still unsettles me.
do: Bring **two rosters** to the shift committee.
Postpone the **kitchen** if my hours fall.
Apply after **actual cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering operator work.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible loss of paid hours.
S1.quote: I would be anxious about my hours, though I have options.
fieldNote: Her **collective bargaining** focuses on paid time, job transfers and safe guards.
The training place is a **request only**; the kitchen delay and outside application require real cuts and adequate postings.

steps.text: Bring two rosters to union shift committee for written transfer terms
Postpone kitchen purchase if own paid hours fall
Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering operator job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union branch that thinking AGI might arrive in 2028, but capable hands-on robots come around 2031. We need binding paid-hour and safety terms before a robot takes the bumper line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my moulding hours to collapse once those robots can clear jams and inspect clips, even if planning software changes earlier. Our year of savings and flat rent could bridge a while, but the tenant may lose work too; I would lie awake adding up the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid press shifts while they exist and bring staffing figures to the branch each week. If hours are cut, I would stop the kitchen purchase, apply for posted reachable factory work paying enough for our bills, and ask the union to campaign for wage support; I would not spend the education money on a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the expected big wage loss. Having assets does not make a family immune to a whole line closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a public protest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the branch calls one, I would go and ask for rules on notice and wage support. I would carry the roster showing which paid shifts disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the rented flat solve the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the tenant’s rent is useful but not guaranteed. If their work goes too, the flat has costs without the income.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would seek **binding staffing terms** before a line is automated.
think: I expect **most moulding hours** to disappear after capable robots arrive.
Our **flat rent** and savings may not bridge a broad wage loss.
do: Keep **paid press shifts** and bring staffing figures to the branch.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable bill-covering factory work.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage sums.
S2.quote: Our year of savings and flat rent could bridge a while, but the tenant may lose work too; I would lie awake adding up the mortgage.
fieldNote: She expects **physical automation** to end most press hours around 2031, after thinking AGI.
Her **rental income** can fail with the tenant’s job; union action and local applications have explicit triggers.

steps.text: Bring staffing figures to union branch each week
Cancel kitchen purchase after paid hours are cut
Apply after lost hours for posted reachable bill-covering factory job
Join branch protest for wage support if called

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable press robots around 2034 give us five years to bargain. I want a wage-backed transfer agreement, not a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight, I will still have school costs and perhaps the mortgage. I know I might spend a year hoping the robot plan disappears; Tomas would make me look at the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stand for shop steward this year and put fresh surplus from full wage months against the mortgage. If the company offers a funded quality-inspection qualification on paid shifts, with a stopped-machine practice place and a posted reachable role at bill-covering pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years gives me a bargaining calendar. I would rather learn to inspect a real rejected clip than sit through an unpaid slide show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is offered without a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my press shift and ask for a written list of actual openings. We can afford to wait for an adequate job, but I will not buy a certificate for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a steward do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would collect shift-by-shift counts of paid setup and inspection time, then take them to management with our branch. Gül can help check the figures.

say: I would demand a **wage-backed transfer** before 2034 robots.
I would take **paid inspection time** to the union table.
think: The **mortgage and school costs** may remain at forty-eight.
My **own delay** could waste a year unless Tomas pushes me.
do: Stand for **shop steward** and collect paid-time figures.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh full-month wage surplus.
Enrol in **funded paid quality training** only with safe practice and an adequate posted role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to bargain and check a real offer.
S3.quote: I would rather learn to inspect a real rejected clip than sit through an unpaid slide show.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to new technology** permits a practical qualification only with paid instruction and a real post.
The later **application** follows qualification and requires a posted reachable role at bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Stand for shop steward and collect paid inspection figures
Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full-month wages
Enrol only with funded paid stopped-machine practice and posted reachable bill-covering inspection role
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering inspection role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable factory robots around 2039 leave time for a proper agreement. We should start the bargaining while the line still needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three and fifty-six I may have less mortgage debt, but the children’s needs and my health are not fixed by a date. I do not know whether the flat will still have a paying tenant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep my press shifts, add fresh overtime pay to the study account when offered, and work on a union retraining agreement. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual rosters and posted nearby jobs; if hours fall, I would apply only where pay covers our bills and the work is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant machines and steady about our present money. Ten years lets me finish the mortgage only if the wages actually keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an early pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union what any scheme pays, but I cannot promise to stop working from a brochure. Tomas and I would need to see real household income and the mortgage balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What agreement matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid training and a written vacancy process before any shift is removed. An older worker needs a real chance at a job, not a farewell speech.

say: I would ask for **paid retraining terms** while the line still runs.
I would keep **2036 AI** separate from 2039 press robots.
think: Our **mortgage and tenant rent** may change before I turn fifty-six.
The long calendar cannot guarantee **paid work** or health.
do: Keep **2026 press shifts** and save fresh offered overtime.
Work on a **union vacancy agreement** before cuts.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current finances remain steady.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me finish the mortgage only if the wages actually keep coming.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** justifies unease rather than immediate income fear in the long scenario.
Post-2036 roster checks require **continued employment**; pension questions are information gathering, not a retirement decision.

steps.text: Keep current press shifts and save fresh offered overtime
Work with union on paid training and written vacancy agreement
Apply after cuts for posted reachable safe bill-covering job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove most of our press hours before the children finish school. A funded wage-backed transfer, written job postings and a union seat before equipment decisions would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the order for a robot cell. I can argue with a manager at a table; I cannot bargain with a machine.

headlineQuote: I can argue with a manager at a table; I cannot bargain with a machine.
portrait: **Sara**, 43, operates car-parts moulding presses with a vocational certificate, strong earnings and sixteen years of experience.
Her **bus-driver partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, year-plus reserve and rented flat give her room to bargain and choose.
She has **never used AI**, distrusts untested screens and brings paid-time and safety records to her union committee.
Fast robots threaten **press hours**, while longer warning permits conditional inspection training and extra mortgage payments from wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time to protect press wages before capable robots reach the line around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage-backed transfer**, posted adequate jobs and union involvement before equipment decisions would help.
